When you cross through the threshold of his medical division, you're no longer an inmate, you are a patient. And he has his whole team focused on being patient advocates. He's been the medical director at Chesterfield County Jail for over 22 years. And I will tell you, to what you said, Dr. Gay, is really important.

We are fortunate that Chesterfield County allows us to employ our own medical doctor at the jail. I will say that the majority, far majority of jails in Virginia and beyond employ contracted doctors. And like it or not, sometimes they work towards the contract, not towards the patient.

Item 5, Work Sessions. A, Sheriff's Office Annual Update. Sheriff Leonard. Hear anybody there?

We'll start over. No, we won't. But thank you for the opportunity to provide the update. We are an organization of 325 of the most amazing people serving this county in our community. While the nation celebrates its 250th birthday this year, Chesville County Sheriff's Office has been serving for over 277 years now, not me personally.

Today I want to focus on everything that is good with the Chesville Sheriff's Office, but I would be remiss if I did not highlight some of the negative external impacts we are dealing with. I will keep this just one slide as I would like to dedicate the rest of my time to focus on more of the stuff that is right in the Sheriff's Office, which is plenty.

This slide consolidates everything we presented during our budget presentation several weeks ago. This is all information I know you are all familiar with. The short of it is, as this county continues to grow, our workloads are growing proportionally to that, and it results in more work demands, the need for more personnel, all at a time where we're seeing the cost for services increase at even a quicker pace.

Through it all, we continue to deliver a high level of service without interruption to our customers or community members. I am joined, by the way, with Lieutenant Colonel Matt Wilkerson, the chief deputy. You got it? I got it. He's got control. So, you know, speaking of everything that's good with the sheriff's office, again, we did complete our main courthouse, Sallyport.

That was a lengthy project that was much needed. Before, and if you look at that square right roof, everything there is brand new. Before that was there, we had a single garage entry to embark or disembark inmates going to court.

We have dozens and dozens of people have to be moved to the courthouse every day for court appearances in our many different courtrooms. The new courthouse, as it is affectionately known, is 37 years old. The single bay created for the Sally Port that was there before this was designed for vehicles 37 years ago.

The new vans we use today could barely fit into there. And everybody that pulled in had to back out. You couldn't fit two in there at the same time. That caused a backup of vans lined up in our parking lot loaded with inmates from various jails, including Riverside, Chessville, and across the state, all waiting to be unloaded.

We had employees walking through the parking lot. The inmates in these vans would watch them, see where they parked the cars. It just was not a safe environment. We are fortunate the county supported the building of this. You can actually fit 16 vehicles in this alley port.

We went from 1 to 16. It expedites the offload and onload of inmates. It creates a much safer environment for all employees, not just those at the sheriff's office. Next slide. One of the things we learned through that construction was a temporary fence was erected to stop people from going through the construction site.

It proved to be such a great security barrier for us to create an intact zone behind the courthouse for our employees, especially judges who park out there, That when the project is over, we decided to go ahead and erect this permanent privacy fence around the parking lot.

You can go to the next slide. You see this really segregates that area between the two courthouses for our employees to park in safety without concern of anybody coming through the two. We've had a lot of foot traffic between the two courthouses in the past.

As you know, we just had somebody on foot the other night who did some damage to our courthouse walking through the front. It's not unusual to have people walking all hours of the days. After this was constructed, all the judges were in agreement that they felt much safer. This was a great needed addition for the courthouse, and we're happy to have it there.

So I want to focus on our employees, a diverse group of individuals working together as a team, as a family, towards the same mission, to enhance public safety, providing a safe court environment, the service of legal documents, and comprehensive care of offenders through professional and unbiased performance. In this way, the Sheriff's Office fully supports and fosters Chessfield's efforts to be an extraordinary and innovative community in which to live, work, and play.

And if you look at the map up there, that's all the different countries our Sheriff's Office employees come from, where they were born. And it is our diversity that makes us the great organization we are today. Speaking of our people, we look at our demographics here in Chessfield County compared to the demographics of our sheriff's office. As you can see in our sheriff's office, we really believe in diversity and we show that throughout our ranks and throughout our personnel in civilian and sworn alike. And sworn on the far right, you'll see the actual

demographics for sworn personnel far exceeding what the county demographics are. And that's our goal is to be reflective or beyond reflective of the community we serve. Has anybody heard of the 30 by 30 initiative. This is a national initiative aimed at increasing the representation of women in law enforcement, sworn positions specifically, to 30 percent by the year 2030. Chesville County is well on its way to getting here. Next slide. Today we have 25 percent of our entire force is

female, but I'm proud to say, go next slide, that 23 percent of our leadership positions are held by females at this point. So we're well on our way to reaching that 30 by 30 initiative, which we expect to be achieved long before 2030. Next slide. Keeping in the theme when we recognized Dr. Gay earlier today, I would like to solely focus on our civilian employees. Often lost in the mix and overshadowed by our sworn compliment, they are critical and crucial to our success as any other employees. And that's what I wanted to do for the rest of this presentation. And I'm just

going to go through a couple of them really quick. Our criminal information unit, our records room, Handling all the papers that get issued, they all have to be entered, they all have to be filed. Behind them is a rack of 3,500 warrants to be served in Chesterfield County. There are a lot of papers that come through here. Their work is essential and critical.

The timing, and the board a few years ago, if you recall, allowed us to staff a 24-hour, 24-7 operation. This is critical because we don't want to wait to enter a paper into the computer. So a police officer, a trooper in Texas stops a car for somebody who's wanted on a serious crime here, doesn't get that information timely.

So now with having 24-7 operations, those papers are entered within minutes of us receiving them. They go into a nationwide database, hopefully providing a safer environment for everybody out there. The next is our mental health team. Again, we are privileged in Chesterfield County to have support of the board.

Most jails do not invest in mental health. We are blessed to have the mental health team we have in our jail. They provide essential service to our folks. I was talking to somebody yesterday about our jail population having 70% population of people with mental illness.

I was corrected. 90% of our population has mental illness in our jail. That's what we've become because of lack of other resources on the outside. To have those folks in our jail and not attend to their mental health needs, I think would be a disservice to all of them in our community.

So, again, we're very blessed to have a mental health team that focuses on the mental health of our inmates. Next is our programs and rehabilitation team. You know, again, this is, HARP is just one piece of this. This includes a lot of other things they do from GED to other skills training, getting people into community colleges, which we do, and things like that.

Our goal is to rehabilitate, get people the skills, abilities, and tools to succeed when they're released. And, again, this is a critical part of our organization. Next is our medical team. Dr. Gay there front and center. I know he's very proud of his team. I can't say enough about them. It's tough to be a nurse in any profession. But when you ask somebody to do their profession inside the confines of a jail, understand that they're locked up for their whole shift. You can't get in and out of the jail like you can any other job. So we're blessed to have a dedicated team on our medical staff.

And then our security specialists are another civilian part of our program that's really been helpful to us. We are implementing more of these positions now within the jail so we can save having to hire more deputies, identifying more jobs they can actually do at their level without being sworn.

They don't have the training that deputies go through. They don't get the equipment that deputies go through. But there's a number of functions that they can provide to us, which really provide a cost savings to everybody. And then our newest endeavor is COMPASS, Comprehensive Opioid Management and Patient Assistance for Substance Support.

It's a long word. I think Dr. Gay came up with this acronym for us. You know, we have a lot of acronyms in our program. We have HARP, we have SMART, and now we have COMPASS. We're very excited about COMPASS. It just launched about two, three weeks ago. And, you know, it's a new and complimentary piece of Chesterfield County Jail's existing HARP and SMART program.

SMART is Supported Medically Assisted Rehabilitative Treatment Program, another Dr. Gay acronym. It only serves inmates who serve from substance use disorder and have pre-existing prescriptions for MAT or MOUD. Where, you go to the next one, COMPASS will allow the Chesterfield County Jail to screen all incoming inmates for substance use disorder and support the full continuum of care for MOUD regimen and medically assisted treatment.

Induction, withdrawal, and maintenance. it also allows us to fill the gap in services for those who enter the jail but are released within hours we're going to try to capture everybody who is in that short window and get them the help they need on an mat program substance use disorder is complicated disease with no one pathway to long term treatment or recovery it requires an individualized roadmap roadmap for care compass will also provide substance use support services to inmates in the general population of jail who who are not part of HARP.

This allows for a multifaceted continuum of care per Title II of the ADA, requiring that correctional facilities provide MAT for inmates with opiate use disorder. Now to the challenges, I mentioned mental health before.

We have what's called a one-on-one when somebody is a serious threat to harm themselves. We are seeing more and more of this. When we have a one-on-one situation, I have to put a deputy one-on-one with that individual with eyes on. They must maintain eyes on at all times.

They can't leave to respond to an emergency. They can't leave to do anything else. They have to remain there one-on-one. This takes a deputy out of our rotation for all the other security needs we have in the jail while we're running operations. If you see the picture on the far right, that one particular incident, we had two people on 101s.

That's two deputies off the shift who can do nothing but just watch the individual for their safety and concern. So mental health is the number one failure in this nation, and we have a long way to go to address it. And right now, jails, unfortunately, have been the collecting point for people suffering from that disease of mental health.

We are trying our best to help them. So that's a big challenge for us right now. Next, you probably all have seen or heard or been inconvenienced by the HVAC overall at the jail. While the new courthouse is 37 years old, the jail celebrates their 20th birthday this year.

As I always said to the board, jails age like dog ears. It's not a traditional building because of the way it's constructed. A 20-year-old jail really has seen the wear and tear of about a 60-year-old building. This HAC overhaul is much needed. It's well overdue, but it is causing a lot of interruptions with services.

And unfortunately, a cost to our taxpayers in that, like right now, I have one entire side of the jail closed. That's over 100 inmates that have to be at Riverside at per diem rate we're paying for Riverside and not in our jail because all those beds are remaining open while they're doing the overhead work.

That's unexpected costs I don't think we saw coming into this project. It's a two-year-plus project, supposed to be finished in September, but just like today when one thing that was supposed to finish on Thursday is now extended to next week, it's got a lot of pushback, and we're waiting to see where we go with this.

The next challenge is back at the new courthouse, the main courthouse. Again, these are inmate movement elevators. There's only three of them in the entire building. All three are 37 years old. There is only one way to get inmates from holding in the basement up to the 10, 12 courtrooms.

Keep adding courtrooms. I don't know where we are today. So I think it's 12 courtrooms currently. The only way to get inmates in custody up for trial is through these elevators. None of them work at this point. And when I say don't work, they do go up and down, but the security doors do not close.

So now every time we put somebody on there, we have to put a deputy in there with them to ensure they don't do anything with that. The problem is later this year, all three are scheduled to be replaced. And when we shut these down, it's going to cause an interruption to court services for people that are in custody going to court trial.

We don't know what that timeline is going to be. We don't have a plan right now, but it is going to be a challenge for us later on this year. And then shifting away from consolidated services has been a challenge for us for the last several years. We are continually running out of space, not just the sheriff's office, but all entities working at the new courthouse and running out of space.

And it's a matter of robbing from Peter to pay Paul. And we're doing our share by moving to off-site locations. That, moving everybody out from being consolidated has helped hurt us with services, excuse me. And I will, you go to the next slide.

This is just a picture of all the different facilities we operate out of now. The Cogbill building, the old Parks and Rec building, I forget what you call the other building, Clay, where civil process is, the remote work center.

We're all over the map now with our personnel. We'd like to reconsolidate down the road. We know that that's possible when we get through this expansion, whenever that occurs. So right now it is a challenge for us. And then space inside the jail has also been hard to find.

This is our compass crew. This is where they're operating out of. It's one of the indoor rec centers for our inmates. This is also where we do medically-assisted treatment. So we're using space dedicated for some other use. Actually, we have five desks in there, computers, and phones to operate out of this because we are out of space at the jail as well.

And then the last challenge is going to be our hiring. We are struggling right now to hire deputies as well as civilians. In fact, we had an academy scheduled to begin on February 4th. We had to cancel that academy because we could not fill it.

We cannot meet the minimum required by DCJS, which is five, to actually start an academy. We're having a little struggle hiring people right now, both on the sworn and the civilian side. We do fill a lot of civilian positions.

They tend to stay for about two weeks and then leave for a private sector job. For instance, the transportation coordinator, we've been through three of them in the last three months. They keep taking a job and then leaving a job for other jobs. So right now hiring is a little bit of a challenge for us.

But I will say that in the scheme of things, I do not stress over where we are. We are, I think, Captain Phillips, we're at eight sworn vacancies down right now. I don't like having eight vacancies, but when I talk to my peers, they would all love to have eight vacancies.

Other jurisdictions are in the hundreds and beyond when it comes to personnel shortages. So to only have eight right now is a blessing, but we like to be fully staffed. And with that, we're just going to leave you with the faces of our sheriff's office, and I open it up for any questions.

Board, any questions? I have just a couple in that you said you're eight vacancies down right now. I'm curious to know, have you done a count on how many people, I mean, kind of picking up on what Mr. Engel is saying, that are getting close to retirement?

Yeah, we've done surveys on that. And I think right now we have over 30 people that could retire today, any moment. And we do a survey about every six months to assess that. And it's been pretty accurate. Like we had one that was scheduled to retire sometime before August.

And sure enough, that came to fruition. And we're losing quite a bit of our command staff as well between now and into the year. And then what do you think is the barrier right now for hiring or sending someone through the academy or through the training?

I don't know if there's a barrier. We're getting applications, but most of the applications are being disqualified before they even get anywhere into the process. DCGS has a list of automatic disqualifiers. It's beyond our control.

The state controls that. There's a lot that we can't even move forward in the process because of some things in the past. So we do get a lot of applications. Unfortunately, they're not able to get through the background to move forward in the process. And I do want to say real quick, if I can take this minute, we are making some promotions August 1st.
